\chapter{La Casa --- Your First Everyday Noun}
\label{ch:noun-casa}
\hlchaptermodality{69}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say la casa and tengo una casa, using the article and gender rules I already hold.}

Complete ES-C43-casa: produce la casa and tengo una casa, and say what casa meant in Latin.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la casa]{la casa — \textquotedblleft{}house,\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}home\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C43-casa}



\begin{quote}
You have spent a long time learning what to \textbf{do} with nouns — their gender, their articles, their agreement. This chapter and the next few hand you some nouns to do it with.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{s-sound} — the \emph{s} in \emph{casa} is a plain, unvoiced \emph{s}. Spanish has no \emph{z} buzz here: \emph{KAH-sah}, never \emph{KAH-zah}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{la casa} — \emph{the house}, and just as often \emph{home}.
\end{quote}

Latin \textbf{casa} meant something humbler than a house: a \textbf{hut}, a cottage, the small shelter a farm worker lived in. The grand Latin word for a proper house was \emph{domus} — which is where \textbf{domestic} and \textbf{dome} come from. And \emph{domus} lost. Across the whole west of the Roman world the humble word won and the grand one faded: Spanish \emph{casa}, Italian \emph{casa}, Portuguese \emph{casa}.

French took the same word somewhere stranger. \emph{Casa} wore down until it stopped being a noun at all and became the little word \textbf{chez} — so \emph{chez moi} is, underneath, \textquotedblleft{}at the house of me.\textquotedblright{}

Italian kept a small one too: \emph{casino} is \emph{casa} plus a diminutive ending — literally \textquotedblleft{}little house.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a feminine noun, behaving exactly as promised}]
\emph{Casa} ends in \emph{-a} and is feminine, so it takes \textbf{la}. That is the common case, and it is worth having one plain example on hand before you meet the awkward ones.

\begin{quote}
\emph{la casa} — the house. \emph{Tengo una casa.} — I have a house.
\end{quote}

Nothing new is happening here. That is the point: the machinery has been ready for a long time, and this is the first ordinary thing to run through it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}la casa\textquotedblright{} — \emph{KAH-sah}, a clean \emph{s}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Tengo una casa\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}the house\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{La casa}}.) What did \emph{casa} mean in Latin? (A \textbf{hut} — the humble word that outlived the grand one.) Next: a masculine noun whose Latin ancestor was a piece of a tree.
\end{tcolorbox}
